moments.body: 2007: Joe Wright's adaptation. Strong critical reception; six Oscar nominations (one win — best original score). The film's Dunkirk beach tracking shot became a celebrated technical achievement.
moments.takeaway: The film made the novel accessible to a wider audience and intensified its presence in popular culture.

now.title: Contemporary British fiction
now.body: Atonement is one of the most-taught contemporary British novels at A-level and university. Its formal experimentation, its WWII setting, and its metafictional ending all give classrooms much to discuss. McEwan's prose style — precise, lucid, ironic — has shaped a generation of British fiction.
now.open_questions: Does Briony's 'atonement' work? She gives her lovers a happy ending in fiction they were denied in reality. The novel makes us question what fiction can do morally.

items.reflection: A novel about a child's lie, the cost of false witness, and the limits of fictional atonement has become a touchstone of 21st-century English literature. McEwan's combination of precise prose, deep moral seriousness and formal play makes Atonement one of the most ambitious recent British novels.

moments.title: Never Let Me Go published
moments.body: March 2005: Never Let Me Go published. The novel follows three friends — Kathy, Tommy, Ruth — who grow up at the Hailsham boarding school in an alternative 1990s England where they have been bred as organ donors. The donations begin in their twenties.
moments.takeaway: Ishiguro's restraint — the horror is implied rather than dramatised — is the novel's defining technique. The characters know their fate but speak about it gently.

moments.title: Mark Romanek film
moments.who: Carey Mulligan, Keira Knightley, Andrew Garfield
moments.body: 2010: Mark Romanek's film adaptation. Strong performances; the film's commercial reception was muted but critical reception was strong. The film made the novel accessible to wider audiences.
moments.takeaway: Ishiguro had supervised the screenplay (Alex Garland). His film involvement is unusual for major novelists.

moments.title: Nobel Prize
moments.body: 2017: Ishiguro wins the Nobel Prize in Literature, 'who, in novels of great emotional force, has uncovered the abyss beneath our illusory sense of connection with the world'. His earlier novels — The Remains of the Day (1989, Booker), An Artist of the Floating World (1986), When We Were Orphans (2000) — established his reputation.
moments.takeaway: Ishiguro had grown up in Britain (his Japanese family emigrated when he was 5). His work explores memory, dignity and self-deception across cultures.

now.title: Bioethics in fiction
now.body: Never Let Me Go is taught at A-level and undergraduate level. Its themes — bioethics, the trap of acceptance, the ethics of using one class of humans as means for another — resonate with modern debates about reproductive technology, AI, surrogacy, organ trafficking. The novel's quiet horror has only become more relevant.
now.open_questions: Why don't the characters resist? Critics have asked whether Ishiguro's restraint is the novel's strength or weakness. The acceptance itself is part of his subject.

items.reflection: A dystopia presented through the gentlest prose, about young people raised for organ donation. Ishiguro's combination of restraint and devastation makes Never Let Me Go one of the most haunting novels of the 21st century. Its formal grace serves its moral force.

moments.title: Practical Criticism
moments.body: 1929: I.A. Richards publishes Practical Criticism — an experiment in which he gave undergraduates unsigned poems and analysed their responses. The book argues for close attention to the text itself rather than biographical or historical context. The foundation of close reading.
moments.takeaway: Richards (with Charles Ogden) had also written The Meaning of Meaning (1923). His work is foundational to 20th-century English literary studies.

moments.title: Empson's Seven Types of Ambiguity
moments.body: 1930: William Empson, an undergraduate at Cambridge, publishes Seven Types of Ambiguity. Close reading of poetic ambiguity — multiple meanings simultaneously held — as the source of poetic power. The book remains a classic.
moments.takeaway: Empson's argument: ambiguity is not a defect but a strength of poetry. The book is the foundation of modern poetic interpretation.

moments.title: New Criticism in America
moments.who: John Crowe Ransom, Cleanth Brooks, Robert Penn Warren
moments.body: American New Criticism — Ransom's 'The New Criticism' (1941), Brooks's 'The Well Wrought Urn' (1947), Brooks and Warren's textbook 'Understanding Poetry' (1938) — dominates US English departments for two decades. Close reading of the text without biographical or historical context.
moments.takeaway: Wimsatt and Beardsley's 'Intentional Fallacy' (1946) and 'Affective Fallacy' (1949) reject appeal to authorial intent or reader emotion.

now.title: After New Criticism
now.body: New Criticism dominated until structuralism (1960s), poststructuralism (1970s), New Historicism (1980s), and contemporary cultural studies displaced it. But close reading remains the foundation of literary study — even theoretical movements that reject formalism still practice close attention to texts.
now.open_questions: Can close reading be separated from historical context? Recent critics (Franco Moretti, distant reading) propose computational alternatives. The debate continues.

items.reflection: A set of Cambridge and American mid-20th-century critics taught generations how to read poetry. Whether or not we still accept the New Critical theory, the practice of close reading remains central to the discipline they shaped.

moments.title: A Room of One's Own
moments.body: 1929: Woolf's foundational essay argues that material conditions (income, private space) determine women's literary production. The fictional Judith Shakespeare — Shakespeare's equally talented sister — would have been driven to suicide by lack of education and opportunity.
moments.takeaway: Woolf's essay sat largely unrecognised as theory until second-wave feminism in the 1970s.

moments.title: Second-wave feminist criticism
moments.who: Kate Millett, Mary Ellmann, Elaine Showalter
moments.body: Millett's 'Sexual Politics' (1970), Ellmann's 'Thinking About Women' (1968), Showalter's 'A Literature of Their Own' (1977). The feminist project — recover women writers excluded from the canon, expose patriarchal assumptions in male-authored canonical texts.
moments.takeaway: Showalter's coinage 'gynocriticism' distinguished the recovery project from feminist critique of male texts.

moments.title: Gilbert and Gubar's Madwoman in the Attic
moments.body: 1979: 'The Madwoman in the Attic: The Woman Writer and the Nineteenth-Century Literary Imagination'. The argument: 19th-century women writers (Brontë, Eliot, Dickinson) constructed alternative figures — angels and madwomen — to express what patriarchal aesthetics denied them. The book is a foundational text of feminist criticism.
moments.takeaway: Gilbert and Gubar's 'anxiety of authorship' adapts Harold Bloom's 'anxiety of influence' for women writers.

now.title: Feminist criticism now
now.body: Feminist criticism is now woven into mainstream literary study. Intersectional approaches (Crenshaw, bell hooks, Audre Lorde) extended the feminist project to race, class, sexuality. Trans literary criticism, queer feminism, ecofeminism continue to develop the framework.
now.open_questions: Is feminist criticism still a separate field or fully integrated? Many feminist critics argue it should disappear once its concerns are fully absorbed; others see continuing structural patriarchy in publishing and curriculum.

items.reflection: Feminist literary criticism reshaped what counts as literature, what questions to ask of texts, and who the canon serves. Its impact — on syllabuses, anthologies, prize lists, criticism — has been one of the most consequential intellectual shifts in the discipline.

moments.title: Orientalism
moments.body: 1978: Edward Said's 'Orientalism' is published. The argument: Western scholarly and literary representations of the Middle East and Asia have constructed an essentialised 'Orient' that serves Western imperial purposes. The book founds postcolonial studies.
moments.takeaway: Said's work draws on Foucault (discourse, power-knowledge) and Gramsci (hegemony) to analyse literary and scholarly texts as part of colonial power.

moments.title: Spivak's 'Can the Subaltern Speak?'
moments.body: 1985: Spivak's essay 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' interrogates whether colonial subjects can speak at all within structures shaped by colonial discourse. The case of Bhubaneswari Bhaduri's suicide is a centrepiece. The essay is one of the most influential and contested in postcolonial theory.
moments.takeaway: Spivak's translation of Derrida (Of Grammatology, 1976) and her own work straddle deconstruction and postcolonialism.

moments.title: Bhabha's Location of Culture
moments.body: 1994: Bhabha's 'The Location of Culture' develops hybridity, mimicry, the third space. Postcolonial identity is not a return to pre-colonial authenticity but a hybrid space created by colonial encounter. The framework has been influential and contested.
moments.takeaway: Said, Spivak and Bhabha are sometimes called the 'holy trinity' of postcolonial theory. Their distinct approaches define the field.

now.title: After empire
now.body: Postcolonial criticism has reshaped literary studies. Achebe's response to Conrad, the recovery of colonial-era writing in colonised countries, the analysis of British canonical texts as imperial texts — all are now mainstream. Decolonising the curriculum is an active 21st-century debate.
now.open_questions: Is postcolonial criticism still useful or has it been absorbed? Critics on both sides argue. The framework has shaped how we read everything from Shakespeare to contemporary novels.

items.reflection: An Egyptian-American scholar and his successors reshaped how literature is read worldwide. The recognition that texts participate in imperial power — even canonical aesthetic texts — opened up a continuing programme of critical reading and curricular reform.

moments.title: Sedgwick's Epistemology of the Closet
moments.body: 1990: Sedgwick's 'Epistemology of the Closet' argues that the homosexual/heterosexual binary structures modern Western thought far beyond the question of sexuality. Sedgwick's earlier 'Between Men' (1985) had introduced homosocial desire to mainstream criticism.
moments.takeaway: Sedgwick's work crystallised what became queer theory. Her death (2009) was a major loss to the field.

moments.title: Butler's Gender Trouble
moments.body: 1990: Butler's 'Gender Trouble' argues gender is performative — produced through repeated acts rather than expressing pre-existing identity. The argument has been variously read as constructivist, deconstructive, and emancipatory.
moments.takeaway: Butler's later 'Bodies That Matter' (1993) responded to misreadings of performativity as voluntarist (we could simply choose another gender). The performativity argument is more structural than that.

moments.title: 'Queer' as theory term
moments.body: 1991: 'Queer Theory: An Introduction' (a conference and special issue of differences edited by Teresa de Lauretis) gives the field its name. The reclamation of 'queer' as theoretical and political term marked a generation of work.
moments.takeaway: Queer theory drew on AIDS-crisis activism and academic poststructuralism — both were essential to its emergence.

now.title: Queer in the academy and beyond
now.body: Queer theory now encompasses queer of colour critique (Roderick Ferguson, José Esteban Muñoz), transgender theory (Susan Stryker, Jack Halberstam), affect theory (Sara Ahmed). The terminology has entered mainstream — 'queer' as identifier, 'queering' as verb. Backlash and trans-exclusionary politics make the questions politically live.
now.open_questions: Is queer theory still useful or has it been absorbed/depoliticised? The questions of how academic theory connects to lived politics remain live.

items.reflection: A set of academic interventions in 1990 reshaped not only literary criticism but how identity and gender are understood broadly. Queer theory's combination of academic rigour and political stake has been one of the most consequential humanities developments of the late 20th century.

moments.title: Faerie Queene published
moments.body: 1590: Books 1-3 of The Faerie Queene published. 1596: Books 4-6. Spenser planned twelve books but completed only six. The poem allegorises Elizabethan virtues, religious controversy and political theory through a romance frame.
moments.takeaway: Spenser invented the 'Spenserian stanza' (8 iambic pentameters + 1 alexandrine, rhyme ababbcbcc). Used later by Byron, Shelley, Keats, Tennyson.

moments.title: Spenser's death
moments.body: Spenser had been an English official in Ireland. His Munster estate (Kilcolman) was destroyed in the Nine Years' War (1598). He returned to London penniless and died there in January 1599. Buried in Westminster Abbey near Chaucer.
moments.takeaway: Spenser's 'A View of the Present State of Ireland' (1596) is one of the most racist texts about Ireland by a major English writer.

moments.title: Reading Spenser
moments.body: Keats began his career imitating Spenser's stanza ('Imitation of Spenser', 1814). His Eve of St Agnes (1820) uses the Spenserian stanza. Wordsworth, Shelley, Byron all engaged with The Faerie Queene.
moments.takeaway: Spenser shaped the Romantic poets who shaped subsequent English verse. The chain of influence is long.

now.title: Spenser now
now.body: Spenser is harder to read than most of his contemporaries — his deliberate archaisms (he aimed for an English that sounded older than it was), his sustained allegory, his length. Modern editions help. The Faerie Queene remains taught at university level.
now.open_questions: How political is the allegory? Each generation has rebalanced. Modern critics emphasise the colonial and Protestant ideological work; older readings emphasised the aesthetic.

items.reflection: The major Elizabethan epic poet wrote a poem so long and so allegorically loaded that most modern readers encounter only excerpts. Spenser's influence on subsequent English verse — his stanza, his diction, his ambition — has been larger than his actual readership.

moments.title: Donne's early career
moments.who: John Donne, Inns of Court and London courts
moments.body: Donne (c. 1572-1631) studied at Oxford, the Inns of Court. He converted from Catholic to Anglican. His early secular love poetry — Songs and Sonnets — was circulated in manuscript. Marriage to Anne More (1601) cost him his court career.
moments.takeaway: Donne's poetry circulated in manuscript during his life and wasn't published until 1633, two years after his death.

moments.title: Donne ordained
moments.who: Donne as Dean of St Paul's
moments.body: Donne was ordained 1615 and became Dean of St Paul's in 1621. His sermons (Donne preached over 160) became some of the most celebrated of the period. His Holy Sonnets and Divine Poems date partly from this period.

quote.text: Death, be not proud.

moments.takeaway: Donne's 'Devotions upon Emergent Occasions' (1624) included 'No man is an island' and 'Ask not for whom the bell tolls' — phrases that have entered English culture.

moments.title: T.S. Eliot's revival
moments.body: 1921: T.S. Eliot's essay 'The Metaphysical Poets' (review of Grierson's anthology) revives interest in Donne and his contemporaries. The 'dissociation of sensibility' thesis argues English poetry lost its capacity for unified thought-feeling after the metaphysicals.
moments.takeaway: Modernist criticism reshaped which 17th-century poets were considered important. Donne moved from being a minor figure to a central one.

now.title: Metaphysical wit
now.body: Donne is now firmly canonical. Modern editions (Helen Gardner's Divine Poems, John Carey's biography, Achsah Guibbory's recent work) sustain serious scholarship. Modern readers find the combination of intellectual wit and emotional intensity attractive.
now.open_questions: Was the 'dissociation of sensibility' real? Eliot's thesis has been substantially criticised. The mid-17th-century English Civil War and the rise of Lockean empiricism are real changes; whether they damaged poetry's capacities is debated.

items.reflection: A poet whose work circulated in manuscript during his lifetime became, three centuries later, a canonical English poet thanks to T.S. Eliot's modernist revival. Donne's combination of metaphysical wit, sexual frankness and religious intensity speaks to modern readers across the gap.

moments.title: Robinson Crusoe
moments.body: 1719: 'The Life and Strange Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe' published in London. Sometimes called the first English novel — though competing claims exist for Bunyan, Behn and others. The book was based partly on the historical Alexander Selkirk (stranded 1704-09 on Juan Fernandez Island).
moments.takeaway: Defoe was a journalist, businessman and government agent before he turned to fiction late in life. Robinson Crusoe was a commercial success.

moments.title: Moll Flanders
moments.body: 1722: 'The Fortunes and Misfortunes of the Famous Moll Flanders' published. A picaresque, autobiographical narrative by a fictional fallen woman. Defoe also published Journal of the Plague Year (1722) and Roxana (1724).
moments.takeaway: Defoe's first-person, prosaic, detail-rich style helped invent the realist novel. He had also published 'A True Relation of the Apparition of One Mrs Veal' (1706) — proto-realist supernatural reportage.

moments.title: Robinsonade
moments.body: Robinson Crusoe spawned the 'Robinsonade' — castaway novels including The Swiss Family Robinson (Wyss, 1812), Coral Island (Ballantyne, 1858), Treasure Island (Stevenson, 1883). Rousseau's Emile (1762) recommended Crusoe as the only book for a child's education.
moments.takeaway: The castaway-civilising-an-island narrative became one of the major European cultural forms, with implications for empire that postcolonial criticism has read carefully.

now.title: Crusoe in postcolonial readings
now.body: JM Coetzee's 'Foe' (1986) reworks the story from Susan Barton's perspective and Friday's silence. Modern readings emphasise colonialism, race, religious labour ethic. The novel's combination of providential narrative and realistic detail remains formally interesting.
now.open_questions: What is Friday's silence? Coetzee made the question central. Crusoe's relationship with Friday has been a focus of postcolonial criticism.

items.reflection: A 1719 castaway narrative shaped the English novel, the colonial imagination, and modern children's literature. Defoe's combination of detail, religious moralism and adventure made the book a foundation — for both literary innovation and ideological work later critics would unpack.

moments.title: Gulliver's Travels published
moments.body: October 1726: 'Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World, by Lemuel Gulliver' published anonymously in London. Four voyages — Lilliput, Brobdingnag, Laputa/Balnibarbi, Houyhnhnm-land. Swift's satire targets political folly, scientific pretension, human nature.
moments.takeaway: Swift was Dean of St Patrick's, Dublin (1713-1745). His satire was both metaphysical and politically specific — 18th-century English politics.

moments.title: A Modest Proposal
moments.body: 1729: 'A Modest Proposal' — Swift suggests Irish poverty could be alleviated by selling Irish babies for food. The savage satire targets English indifference to Irish suffering. The mock-economist tone deceived some readers.

quote.text: A young healthy child well nursed is, at a year old, a most delicious, nourishing, and wholesome food.

moments.takeaway: Swift's Irish writing combined political pamphlet with literary satire. The Drapier's Letters (1724) made him a popular hero in Ireland.

moments.title: Swift's death
moments.body: October 1745: Swift dies after years of declining health. His will left funds to found a hospital for 'idiots and lunatics'. He had described himself in 'On the Death of Dr Swift' (1739) as having 'served human liberty'.
moments.takeaway: Swift's reputation has been variously read — savage misanthrope, moralist, proto-anti-imperialist. Modern criticism (Edward Said, Carol Fabricant) emphasises his colonial Irish context.

now.title: Swift's continuing satire
now.body: Gulliver's Travels has been continuously read as children's adventure, political satire and philosophical fable. Modern reception emphasises the postcolonial context, the satire of empire, and the disturbing fourth voyage (the Houyhnhnms and the Yahoos). It remains widely taught.
now.open_questions: Is Gulliver mad at the end? The Houyhnhnm Land voyage's conclusion — Gulliver preferring horses to humans — has been read as Swift's final position, as Gulliver's pathology, or as ironic critique of misanthropy. The text supports multiple readings.

items.reflection: An Irish-born Anglican clergyman wrote the greatest English satire of the 18th century. Swift's combination of philosophical depth, political specificity, and savage wit makes Gulliver's Travels one of the works that earns rereading at every age.

moments.title: Shelley and Smith write competing sonnets
moments.who: Percy Bysshe Shelley and Horace Smith
moments.body: December 1817: Shelley and his friend Horace Smith have a sonnet-writing competition on the theme of ancient Egyptian power and time's destruction. Both publish in The Examiner — Shelley on 11 January 1818 (under 'Glirastes'), Smith on 1 February.
moments.takeaway: Shelley's poem is celebrated; Smith's almost forgotten. The pairing reveals how Romantic poets responded to news of antiquity (the discovery of Ramses II's bust at Thebes, then en route to British Museum, 1817-21).

moments.title: Ozymandias's afterlife
moments.body: Shelley's 14-line sonnet condenses a meditation on tyranny, decay and art's outlasting of power. Ramses II's throne name Usermaatra was Greekified as Ozymandias. The 'two vast and trunkless legs of stone' and the 'sneer of cold command' became some of the most famous images in English verse.

quote.text: Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!

moments.takeaway: Shelley died in 1822, age 29, drowned off the Italian coast. His political radicalism shaped much of his poetry.

moments.title: Continued resonance
moments.body: Ozymandias has been quoted in countless contexts — from Breaking Bad's penultimate season finale (2013) using the poem as a tagline to political commentary on fallen leaders. Its compression and image-density make it endlessly quotable.
moments.takeaway: GCSE study has made the poem one of the most-read short poems in English.

now.title: Tyranny and time
now.body: Ozymandias is a standard GCSE anthology poem. Its theme — temporal humility — speaks to every generation that encounters fallen empires. Modern readings emphasise Shelley's political radicalism — the sonnet is partly an attack on contemporary British royalty too.
now.open_questions: Who's speaking — the traveller, the sculptor, the inscription, the poet, the historian? The frames within frames are central to the sonnet's force.

items.reflection: Fourteen lines about a broken statue have shaped how English-speakers think about tyranny and time. Shelley's compression, his image of the legs without torso, and his sneer endure because the political pattern they describe endures.

moments.title: The annus mirabilis
moments.body: Spring-autumn 1819: Keats writes his great odes in a few months — Ode to Psyche (April), Ode to a Nightingale (May), Ode on a Grecian Urn (May), Ode on Melancholy (May), Ode on Indolence (May), To Autumn (September). 'La Belle Dame Sans Merci' (April), Lamia, Isabella, the unfinished Hyperion fragments also fall in this period.
moments.takeaway: Few poets in English have written so much of lasting value in so short a time. Keats's letters of the same period are themselves masterworks of literary thought.

moments.title: Keats coughs blood
moments.body: 3 February 1820: Keats wakes coughing blood. As a former medical student he knows what it means — pulmonary tuberculosis. He understood he was dying. His letters of the next year are devastating to read.
moments.takeaway: Keats had nursed his brother Tom through TB death in 1818. Now he himself had it.

moments.title: Keats dies in Rome
moments.body: 23 February 1821: Keats dies in Rome at 25, attended by his friend Joseph Severn. He had asked for an unmarked grave inscribed 'Here lies one whose name was writ in water'. The Protestant Cemetery, Rome, holds him.

quote.text: Beauty is truth, truth beauty.
quote.attrib: Keats, Ode on a Grecian Urn

moments.takeaway: Shelley followed Keats to early death (1822), Byron (1824). The Romantic generation was nearly all gone by the mid-1820s.

now.title: Keats in modern poetry
now.body: Keats is central to A-level and university poetry teaching. Modern readers find in him both technical mastery (the odes' stanza forms, the densely sensual language) and emotional depth. The letters (especially on 'negative capability') remain key in modern poetic theory.
now.open_questions: Is To Autumn the greatest short poem in English? Many readers and critics think so. Its acceptance of mortality, its sensory richness and its formal perfection are sometimes called unmatched.

items.reflection: A young man dying knew he was dying and wrote some of the most beautiful poems in English in the year before he succumbed. Keats's combination of sensual richness, formal mastery and tragic awareness has made him a model for lyric poets ever since.

moments.title: Songs of Innocence
moments.body: 1789: Blake publishes Songs of Innocence in illuminated printing (his own invented technique, etched copper plates). Lyrical poems voiced by children and pastoral figures. 'The Lamb', 'The Little Black Boy', 'Holy Thursday', 'The Chimney Sweeper'.
moments.takeaway: Blake was a printer and engraver; his books were not produced commercially. Few first-edition copies survive — perhaps 20-30.

moments.title: Songs of Experience added
moments.body: 1794: Blake combines Songs of Innocence with new Songs of Experience as 'Two Contrary States of the Human Soul'. 'The Tyger', 'London', 'The Sick Rose', 'A Poison Tree' contrast with parallel Innocence poems. The combined work has been continuously read.

quote.text: Tyger Tyger, burning bright, / In the forests of the night.

moments.takeaway: The illuminated printing means every copy of Blake's books is hand-coloured and slightly different. The visual and textual are inseparable.

moments.title: Jerusalem and the prophetic books
moments.body: Blake's prophetic books — The Marriage of Heaven and Hell (1790), America, Europe, the Four Zoas, Milton (1804-08), Jerusalem (1804-20) — develop a complex personal mythology. He died in 1827, recognised by few contemporaries.
moments.takeaway: Blake's reputation was small in his lifetime. Yeats and Swinburne revived him in the late 19th century. He is now central to Romantic studies.

now.title: Blake's modern presence
now.body: 'Jerusalem' (from Milton's preface, 1808) became Hubert Parry's 1916 anthem and an unofficial English hymn. 'The Tyger' is one of the most-anthologised English poems. Blake's combination of poetry, visual art and political radicalism has shaped subsequent multimedia work.
now.open_questions: How should Blake's complex mythology be read? Northrop Frye's Fearful Symmetry (1947) systematised it; more recent readers have emphasised the political context (French Revolution, Industrial Revolution, the experience of London's poor).

items.reflection: An engraver-poet working in private, virtually unrecognised, produced some of the most influential English poetry and visual art of the past 250 years. Blake's combination of mystical vision, political radicalism and technical innovation continues to find new readers in every generation.

moments.title: Marlowe born
moments.body: 26 February 1564: Marlowe baptised in Canterbury, son of a shoemaker. Educated at the King's School Canterbury and Corpus Christi, Cambridge (MA 1587, after the Privy Council intervened to grant his degree despite his absences — almost certainly for government intelligence work).
moments.takeaway: Marlowe was born two months before Shakespeare. The two parallel careers — Shakespeare developed steadily; Marlowe burned brilliantly and briefly.

moments.title: The plays
moments.body: 1587-93: Tamburlaine the Great (Parts 1 and 2), The Jew of Malta, Doctor Faustus, Edward II, The Massacre at Paris. Blank verse — 'Marlowe's mighty line' (Ben Jonson) — transformed Elizabethan drama. Faustus's pact with Mephistopheles is the canonical Renaissance treatment of the legend.

quote.text: Is this the face that launched a thousand ships?
quote.attrib: Doctor Faustus, on Helen of Troy

moments.takeaway: Marlowe wrote some of the greatest blank verse in English. Shakespeare's early plays show clear Marlovian influence.

moments.title: Marlowe killed
moments.body: 30 May 1593: Marlowe is killed in a Deptford inn during a dispute, allegedly over the bill ('le recknynge'). Ingram Frizer claims self-defence and is pardoned. Marlowe was 29. He had been arrested earlier that month on charges of atheism; some scholars think the death was political assassination.
moments.takeaway: Marlowe was reportedly an atheist, a spy, a member of Walter Raleigh's 'School of Night'. The historical record is fragmentary; the legend is rich.

now.title: Marlowe's continuing reputation
now.body: Doctor Faustus is still performed; Tamburlaine has had major recent productions. Marlowe's plays anticipate Shakespeare in many ways and rival him in others. The First Folio's exclusion of Marlowe's name from the play of Henry VI Part 1 (which he probably co-authored) was corrected in scholarly editions in 2016.
now.open_questions: Did Marlowe write parts of Shakespeare's early history plays? Computational stylometry (Brian Vickers, Gary Taylor) increasingly suggests yes — co-authored with the young Shakespeare. The literary history is being rewritten.

items.reflection: Christopher Marlowe died at 29 with a body of plays that already rivalled anything in English. His death in mysterious circumstances left questions that have never been answered. He shaped what Shakespeare would do — and was nearly Shakespeare's equal in the work he had time to complete.

moments.title: Castle of Otranto
moments.body: December 1764: 'The Castle of Otranto' published. Walpole presented it as the translation of a medieval Italian manuscript. The second edition (1765) admitted he had written it. Subtitle: 'A Gothic Story' — the first use of 'Gothic' as fiction genre.
moments.takeaway: Walpole was the son of Britain's first Prime Minister, Robert Walpole. He built Strawberry Hill — a Gothic Revival villa near Twickenham — that helped popularise the architectural style. The novel followed from the architecture.

moments.title: Gothic explosion
moments.who: Anne Radcliffe, Matthew Lewis, Mary Shelley, Charles Maturin
moments.body: Following Walpole, Gothic fiction floods late 18th-century England. Ann Radcliffe's Mysteries of Udolpho (1794), Matthew Lewis's The Monk (1796), Maturin's Melmoth the Wanderer (1820). The genre's tropes — ruined castles, persecuted heroines, mysterious villains, the past returning — are established.
moments.takeaway: Jane Austen's Northanger Abbey (1817) is a gentle satire of Gothic conventions. The genre was already mature enough to mock.

moments.title: Gothic's transformations
moments.who: Bronte, Stevenson, Stoker, du Maurier, King, Carter
moments.body: Wuthering Heights, Jekyll and Hyde, Dracula, Rebecca (1938), Stephen King's novels, Angela Carter's Bloody Chamber (1979), modern gothic novels by Sarah Waters and others. The Gothic adapts continuously.
moments.takeaway: The Gothic mode has proven one of the most resilient in English fiction — adapting to industrial, psychological, postcolonial, queer and feminist contexts.

now.title: Why Gothic persists
now.body: Modern Gothic — film, novel, video game — is one of the largest popular genres. Its themes (the buried past, persecuted innocence, monstrous power, the uncanny) speak to anxieties that don't disappear. Recent academic Gothic studies (Fred Botting, David Punter) have established the genre's seriousness.
now.open_questions: What is Gothic responding to? Walpole's original wave was partly nostalgia for medieval Catholic emotion in a Protestant age of reason. Subsequent Gothics respond to different things — industrial change, sexual repression, colonial guilt.

items.reflection: A 1764 fake-medieval manuscript spawned one of the most durable English fictional genres. Walpole's antiquarian Gothic became, through hundreds of imitators and reinventions, a permanent mode of fiction — and one capable of addressing the modern world's worst fears.

moments.title: Poetics
moments.body: Around 335 BCE: Aristotle's Poetics is composed as lecture notes. Twenty-six chapters define tragedy as imitation (mimesis) of serious action, complete and of a certain magnitude, in language with artistic embellishments — producing catharsis of pity and fear. The unities of action, time and place are partially implied; later neoclassical critics codified them.
moments.takeaway: The text we have is incomplete. A second book on comedy is referred to but does not survive (the premise of Umberto Eco's 'The Name of the Rose', 1980).

moments.title: Renaissance revival
moments.body: Italian Renaissance critics (Castelvetro, 1570) and then French neoclassicists codified Aristotle's text into the 'three unities' of action, time and place. French classical theatre (Corneille, Racine) followed these rules; Shakespeare emphatically did not.
moments.takeaway: Doctor Johnson's 'Preface to Shakespeare' (1765) attacks the unities as artificial and defends Shakespeare's breaches as serving truth.

moments.title: Catharsis debated
moments.body: The meaning of catharsis has been continuously debated — purgation (Bernays, 1857), clarification (Golden), intellectual recognition. The dispute is not settled. Stephen Halliwell's 'The Aesthetics of Mimesis' (2002) remains a major modern reading.
moments.takeaway: Brecht's modern theatre theory (Verfremdungseffekt) defined itself against Aristotelian catharsis — attempting alienation rather than emotional involvement.

now.title: Poetics now
now.body: The Poetics is still taught in every literary theory course. Its categories — plot, character, diction, thought, spectacle, melody — and concepts (tragic flaw/hamartia, recognition/anagnorisis, reversal/peripeteia) remain in critical vocabulary. Modern application to film and television has been productive.
now.open_questions: Is Aristotle's analysis of tragedy still valid? Modern tragic theory (George Steiner, 'The Death of Tragedy', 1961) has questioned whether tragedy is even possible in modernity. Aristotle's framework still organises much of the discussion.

items.reflection: Notes from 4th-century BCE lectures became the founding text of Western literary theory. Aristotle's Poetics — incomplete, sometimes opaque — has continued to organise how we think about narrative for nearly 2,400 years. Few texts have been more consequential for understanding what stories do.
